subtopic_detail: Mute immobile inpatient with waxy flexibility refusing food for two days
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar asked to review a twenty four year old man admitted eight days ago with a relapse of schizophrenia, whose olanzapine dose was increased four days ago.

For the past two days he has stopped speaking, sits in the same chair for hours and has eaten nothing. Nursing staff report that when they raise his arm to change his shirt it stays in the position they leave it in. He resists passive movement of his neck, repeats the last words said to him and has not passed urine since yesterday. He is afebrile with no rigidity of the limbs and no tremor.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mute with staring and reduced blinking, posturing maintained against gravity, waxy flexibility, negativism on passive neck movement, echolalia when addressed, no lead pipe rigidity, palpable bladder
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 180 units per litre (40-320), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 84 micromol/L (60-110), C reactive protein within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Stop the olanzapine and start bromocriptine with dantrolene for a presumed neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and transfer him to a medical ward for monitoring
options.rationale: He has no fever, no lead pipe rigidity, no autonomic instability and a normal creatine kinase, so the malignant syndrome is not present. Treating it would expose him to dopaminergic and muscle relaxant effects he does not need. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Give a parenteral lorazepam challenge and observe over the following hours for improvement in the mutism and immobility
options.rationale: A benzodiazepine challenge is both the first line treatment and a diagnostic manoeuvre, with a substantial proportion of patients showing partial or complete response within hours. Response also guides the ongoing regimen while the underlying illness is treated. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia

options.text: Increase the olanzapine dose further to treat the underlying psychotic relapse and review him again in twenty four hours after the change
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen this state and raise the risk of progression to a malignant form, and the syndrome emerged after the last dose increase. Escalation is the intervention most likely to convert a treatable syndrome into a life threatening one. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy as the definitive treatment and withhold all other psychotropic medication until the first treatment is given
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is highly effective and is escalated to when benzodiazepines fail or the malignant form develops, but organising it takes time that a simple challenge does not. Withholding the challenge delays a treatment that may work today. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia

options.text: Start intravenous fluids with nasogastric feeding and continue observation, deferring any change in psychotropic medication until he begins speaking again
options.rationale: Supportive care including hydration, prophylaxis against venous thromboembolism and bladder management is necessary but does not treat the syndrome itself. Waiting for spontaneous recovery risks dehydration, pressure injury and thrombosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome rather than a diagnosis and occurs across mood disorders, psychotic disorders and general medical conditions, with mood disorders being the commonest underlying cause overall. Recognition depends on the motor and behavioural signs, including mutism, stupor, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia, echopraxia and stereotypy, and structured instruments such as the Bush Francis scale improve detection. First line treatment is a benzodiazepine challenge, usually lorazepam given parenterally, which produces improvement within hours in a large proportion of cases and serves as a diagnostic test, and doses well above those used for anxiety are often needed without causing sedation. Electroconvulsive therapy is the definitive treatment when benzodiazepines fail or when the malignant form develops with fever and autonomic instability. Antipsychotics may worsen catatonia and can precipitate the malignant form, so continuing to escalate them is the central error to avoid, and supportive care covering hydration, nutrition, pressure areas and thromboprophylaxis runs alongside specific treatment.
key_points: Catatonia is a syndrome with many underlying causes, most often a mood disorder.
A parenteral benzodiazepine challenge is both first line treatment and a diagnostic test.
Doses higher than usual anxiolytic doses are frequently required without causing sedation.
Antipsychotic escalation may worsen the state and risks the malignant form.
Electroconvulsive therapy is definitive when benzodiazepines fail or malignant features appear.
explanation.pearls: Look for urinary retention, deep vein thrombosis and pressure injury at every review of an immobile catatonic patient, because these complications cause much of the mortality attributed to the syndrome and develop silently in someone who cannot report symptoms.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia

subtopic_detail: Refusal of all food because of a delusion that it has been poisoned
stem:
You are the general practitioner making a home visit to a fifty one year old man with a long history of schizophrenia, asked to attend by his sister who lives nearby. He stopped his depot antipsychotic six months ago.

He has eaten almost nothing for five days because he is certain that the water supply and all food in the house have been contaminated by a neighbour who wants him dead. He is drinking small amounts of bottled water that he opens himself. He is alert and oriented, answers questions coherently and says he does not need a doctor because there is nothing wrong with him. He refuses to come to hospital and cannot explain how he will eat safely at home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg lying with a fall on standing, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Thin with dry mucous membranes, weight down 6 kg since a recorded weight four months ago, no focal neurological signs, oriented to time place and person, fixed unshakeable belief about contamination, no insight into the risk of not eating
data_table.Investigations: No recent bloods available, urinalysis shows ketones and concentrated urine on a sample he provided

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Assess his decision making capacity and arrange involuntary assessment under the mental health legislation, organising transport with police assistance if needed
options.rationale: A belief that cannot be reasoned with prevents him from weighing the information relevant to the decision, so the refusal is not a capable one, and there is a serious risk to his health from the untreated mental illness. Involuntary assessment is the lawful pathway to treat that risk. (Source: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance

options.text: Accept his refusal as a capable decision, arrange community mental health follow up this week and ask his sister to bring sealed food that he opens himself
options.rationale: Orientation and coherent speech are not the same as capacity, and he cannot use or weigh information because the delusion determines the conclusion. Deferring while he continues not to eat accepts a preventable deterioration. (Source: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance

options.text: Apply to the guardianship tribunal for a substitute decision maker to consent to admission and treatment on his behalf over the coming days
options.rationale: Guardianship processes operate over days to weeks and are designed for enduring decisions rather than acute psychiatric emergencies. Mental health legislation exists precisely to allow timely assessment in this situation. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance)

options.text: Restart his depot antipsychotic today at his last dose with his sister's consent and review him at home in one week to assess the response to treatment
options.rationale: A relative cannot consent for an adult in this situation, and treating without lawful authority is an assault however well intentioned. Depot medication also takes weeks to act while he remains unable to eat. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance)

options.text: Arrange an urgent ambulance to a medical ward for rehydration and nutrition alone, deferring any psychiatric assessment until his physical state has been corrected
options.rationale: Physical stabilisation is needed but as part of the same admission rather than instead of psychiatric assessment, and a medical ward cannot lawfully detain him if he chooses to leave. The mental illness is what is driving the starvation. (Source: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance

explanation.summary: Capacity is decision specific and is assessed against the ability to understand relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it in the decision and communicate a choice. A patient can be fully oriented and articulate while lacking capacity, because a fixed delusional belief removes the ability to weigh information that contradicts it, and this is the pattern in delusional food refusal. Australian mental health legislation differs in detail between states and territories but shares the core criteria of a mental illness, a serious risk to the health or safety of the person or others, and the absence of a less restrictive option that is reasonably available. Serious risk includes risk from self neglect and starvation, not only risk from self harm or violence. The lawful pathway is assessment under the relevant act, arranged through the local mental health service or emergency department, with police or ambulance assistance for transport where required, and physical stabilisation proceeds alongside rather than instead of psychiatric care.
key_points: Capacity is decision specific and can be absent in an oriented, coherent patient.
A fixed delusion removes the ability to use and weigh relevant information.
Serious risk to health from self neglect satisfies the criteria for involuntary assessment.
Relatives cannot consent to treatment for an adult in this situation.
Guardianship processes are too slow for an acute psychiatric emergency.
explanation.pearls: Document the specific words the patient uses about the risk, because a record showing that he cannot weigh the consequences of not eating is what supports the lawfulness of the decision on later review, and a note that simply states that he lacks insight will not.

sources.label: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance
Australian Law Reform Commission: Equality, capacity and disability

subtopic_detail: Sodium of 121 in a man with schizophrenia who drinks water compulsively through the day
stem:
You are the registrar on the psychiatric inpatient unit called because a forty six year old man with chronic schizophrenia has had a brief generalised seizure. He has been on the ward for three weeks on a stable dose of an antipsychotic.

Staff report that he carries a two litre bottle everywhere, refills it repeatedly at the drinking fountain and has been found drinking from bathroom taps at night. His weight this morning was 3.1 kg higher than the weight recorded when he woke yesterday. He is now drowsy but rousable and has vomited once. He takes no diuretics, has no history of epilepsy and is not on carbamazepine or a serotonergic antidepressant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, no focal neurological deficit, no peripheral oedema, jugular venous pressure not raised, no signs of dehydration, weight up 3.1 kg in twenty four hours
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 121 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urea 2.1 mmol/L (2.5-7.0), creatinine 58 micromol/L (60-110), serum osmolality 254 mosmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 84 mosmol/kg, thyroid function and morning cortisol within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give hypertonic saline as repeated small boluses until the sodium has risen by ten millimoles per litre, then reassess his neurological state and fluid intake
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or coma that are ongoing, given as a small bolus with a strict correction limit, and a rise of ten millimoles in this setting risks osmotic demyelination. His seizure has terminated and he is rousable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start demeclocycline to induce a concentrating defect in the kidney and continue to allow free access to fluids while monitoring the sodium daily
options.rationale: Inducing resistance to antidiuretic hormone treats the wrong mechanism when the hormone is already appropriately suppressed and the urine is maximally dilute. Continued free access to water is the problem that needs addressing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous normal saline with frusemide to remove the excess free water, and review the sodium level after the diuresis has been established
options.rationale: This combination is used for hypervolaemic hyponatraemia with oedema, which he does not have, and it risks rapid overcorrection when water diuresis is already about to occur. Sodium loading is not needed when the total body sodium is normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease the antipsychotic on the assumption that it is causing inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion and observe the sodium over the following days
options.rationale: Drug induced inappropriate secretion produces concentrated urine rather than the maximally dilute urine seen here, so the biochemistry excludes it. Stopping the antipsychotic would also risk relapse of the illness driving the drinking. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Restrict fluid intake with supervision, monitor the sodium frequently during correction and record daily weights to track the fluid balance
options.rationale: Dilute urine with a low serum osmolality shows that the kidney is appropriately excreting a water load that exceeds its capacity, so removing the excess intake is the treatment. Frequent sodium measurement is essential because water diuresis can correct the level dangerously fast once drinking stops. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Primary polydipsia occurs in up to a fifth of people with chronic psychotic illness and becomes dangerous when intake exceeds the renal capacity to excrete free water, which is roughly ten to fifteen litres a day in a healthy adult but is lower in those with impaired solute intake. The biochemical signature is hyponatraemia with a low serum osmolality and maximally dilute urine below one hundred milliosmoles per kilogram, which distinguishes it from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, where the urine is inappropriately concentrated. Rapid diurnal weight gain is the most useful bedside monitor and is more informative than intermittent sodium measurements. Management is supervised fluid restriction with frequent sodium monitoring, because once drinking stops the kidney excretes the water load quickly and the sodium can rise far faster than the safe limit of about eight to ten millimoles per litre in twenty four hours, risking osmotic demyelination. Hypertonic saline is reserved for ongoing seizures or coma and is given in small boluses with strict limits on the rise achieved.
key_points: Urine osmolality below one hundred milliosmoles per kilogram indicates appropriate suppression of antidiuretic hormone.
Inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion produces concentrated rather than dilute urine.
Daily and diurnal weights track water loading better than intermittent sodium levels.
Supervised fluid restriction is the treatment, with frequent sodium monitoring.
Overcorrection is a real risk once drinking stops because a water diuresis follows.
explanation.pearls: Measure the weight on waking and again in the late afternoon, since a diurnal gain above about five per cent of body weight identifies dangerous water loading before the sodium falls, and this simple ward measure prevents more seizures than any biochemical monitoring schedule.

subtopic_detail: Sedation and hypersalivation two weeks after a man stable on clozapine stopped smoking
stem:
You are the doctor in the clozapine clinic reviewing a thirty eight year old man who has been stable on the same dose for four years with no positive symptoms and no admissions.

Two weeks ago he was admitted to a smoke free medical ward for cellulitis and has not smoked since, having previously smoked thirty cigarettes a day. He was started on nicotine replacement patches on the ward and has continued them. His mother says he has been sleeping most of the day, is unsteady when he walks to the toilet and has soaked two pillowcases with saliva each night. He has had no fever, no chest pain and no missed doses.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg lying with a fall on standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy and slow to respond, pooling of saliva with a damp collar, unsteady broad based gait, no rigidity or tremor, chest clear on auscultation, cellulitis resolved
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 4.1 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), C reactive protein within normal limits, electrocardiogram with a corrected QT interval of 428 milliseconds, troponin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe an anticholinergic agent for the hypersalivation and a morning modafinil dose for the sedation, continuing the current clozapine dose unchanged
options.rationale: Treating two symptoms of drug toxicity while leaving the level raised risks seizures, myocarditis surveillance being missed and further deterioration. Symptomatic agents have a place only once the level itself is appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately given the toxicity and start an alternative antipsychotic, arranging review by the treating team in the following week
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation risks cholinergic rebound and rapid psychotic relapse in a man who has been well for four years, and the problem is dose rather than drug. Ceasing for more than two days would also require retitration from the start. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Advise him to resume smoking at his previous level so that the drug level returns to its former range, and review him again in two weeks
options.rationale: Restoring a lethal exposure to manage a drug interaction is indefensible when dose adjustment achieves the same result. Cessation should be supported, with the dose adjusted to match. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Measure the plasma clozapine concentration and reduce the dose in consultation with the treating team, reviewing the sedation and gait after the change
options.rationale: Tobacco smoke induces the enzyme that clears this drug, so stopping smoking raises plasma levels substantially over one to two weeks and produces exactly this toxicity syndrome. Measuring the level confirms the mechanism and guides how far the dose must fall. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Attribute the symptoms to the nicotine replacement patches, cease them and review him in a week to see whether the sedation and salivation have settled
options.rationale: Nicotine itself does not induce the relevant enzyme, which is induced by the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in smoke, so replacement therapy does not protect against the rise in drug level. Stopping it would remove cessation support without altering the cause. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Clozapine is metabolised largely by the cytochrome enzyme CYP1A2, which is induced by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke rather than by nicotine, so smokers require higher doses and levels rise when smoking stops. Plasma concentrations can increase by around fifty per cent or more within one to two weeks of cessation, producing sedation, hypersalivation, ataxia, confusion, postural hypotension and a lowered seizure threshold. The same interaction operates in reverse when a patient resumes smoking after discharge, when levels fall and symptoms can relapse. Admission to a smoke free hospital is therefore a predictable trigger, and services increasingly reduce the dose pre emptively and measure the level within the first fortnight. Other important interactions include fluvoxamine, which inhibits the same enzyme and raises levels sharply, and intercurrent infection, which also raises levels through inflammatory suppression of metabolism.
key_points: Smoke induces CYP1A2, so stopping smoking raises clozapine levels.
Nicotine replacement does not prevent the rise because nicotine is not the inducer.
Levels can rise substantially within one to two weeks of cessation.
Toxicity appears as sedation, hypersalivation, ataxia and a lowered seizure threshold.
Resuming smoking after discharge lowers the level and can precipitate relapse.
explanation.pearls: Missing clozapine for more than about two consecutive days requires retitration from a low dose because of the risk of severe hypotension and collapse on resumption, so an admission that interrupts dosing is as hazardous as one that changes the metabolic environment.

subtopic_detail: Lip smacking and tongue movements after eight years of antipsychotic treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatrist reviewing a fifty nine year old woman with schizophrenia who has taken the same first generation antipsychotic for eight years. Her psychotic symptoms have been well controlled and she lives independently.

Her daughter has noticed repetitive chewing and lip smacking movements over the past six months, which stop briefly when attention is drawn to them and disappear during sleep. The woman herself is not distressed by them but has started avoiding meals out because food falls from her mouth. There is no tremor, no rigidity and no subjective restlessness, and she takes no anticholinergic medication.

data_table.Examination: Repetitive chewing, lip smacking and tongue protrusion, mild choreiform movements of the fingers, no resting tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, no akathisia, gait normal, dentures fit well
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and copper studies within normal limits, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start propranolol titrated to effect for the abnormal movements and review her in six weeks, continuing the current antipsychotic at its present dose
options.rationale: Beta blockade treats akathisia, which is a subjective sense of inner restlessness with an urge to move, and she has none. Choosing a treatment aimed at the wrong movement disorder leaves the real problem progressing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue the current treatment unchanged with six monthly movement rating scales, since she reports no distress and her psychotic illness is well controlled
options.rationale: The movements are already interfering with eating and social participation, and they become irreversible with continued exposure to the causative agent. Monitoring without acting documents deterioration rather than preventing it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Reduce the dose of the current antipsychotic where the illness allows or switch to an agent with lower risk, and consider a vesicular monoamine transporter inhibitor
options.rationale: Reducing exposure to the causative drug class addresses the mechanism, and transporter inhibitors are the only agents with good randomised evidence for suppressing the movements themselves. Both steps are weighed against the risk of psychotic relapse. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Increase the dose of the current antipsychotic, since higher dopamine blockade suppresses the movements and will improve her ability to eat in public
options.rationale: Increasing the dose masks the movements temporarily while worsening the underlying receptor changes, so the problem returns and becomes harder to treat. This is the classic short term fix that causes long term harm. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Start benztropine to counter the abnormal movements and review her in six weeks to assess whether the chewing and lip smacking have improved
options.rationale: Anticholinergic agents treat drug induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia but characteristically worsen these movements, and they add cognitive impairment in an older patient. Withdrawing rather than adding anticholinergic load is the correct direction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Tardive dyskinesia is a delayed onset movement disorder caused by prolonged dopamine receptor blockade, appearing typically after months to years of treatment, and it affects the orofacial region most often with chewing, lip smacking and tongue movements, sometimes extending to choreoathetoid limb and trunk movements. Risk factors include older age, female sex, longer exposure, first generation agents, diabetes and previous acute extrapyramidal reactions. It is distinguished from acute dystonia, which occurs within days, from drug induced parkinsonism, which produces rigidity and tremor, and from akathisia, which is a subjective restlessness, and this distinction matters because anticholinergic agents help the first two while worsening tardive dyskinesia. Management involves reducing or switching the offending antipsychotic where the psychiatric illness permits, withdrawing anticholinergic drugs, and adding a vesicular monoamine transporter inhibitor such as valbenazine or tetrabenazine, which have the best evidence for symptom suppression. Early recognition matters because the condition becomes irreversible with continued exposure, which is why standardised movement scales are performed at regular intervals in long term antipsychotic treatment.
key_points: Onset is delayed by months to years of dopamine receptor blockade.
Orofacial chewing, lip smacking and tongue movements are the typical presentation.
Anticholinergic agents worsen the condition although they help parkinsonism and dystonia.
Reduce or switch the causative agent where the psychiatric illness allows.
Vesicular monoamine transporter inhibitors have the best evidence for suppression.
explanation.pearls: Examine the tongue at rest in the floor of the mouth and ask the patient to hold their hands outstretched and to walk, because early tardive movements are unmasked by distraction and activation manoeuvres and are easily missed in a seated conversational interview.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Neutrophils of 1.2 in a man monitored under a benign ethnic neutropenia protocol on clozapine
stem:
You are the psychiatrist in the clozapine clinic seeing a thirty four year old man of West African ancestry whose treatment resistant schizophrenia has been in remission for three years on clozapine. He works full time and has had no admissions since starting it.

He was registered under a benign ethnic neutropenia protocol two years ago after haematology review, with documented baseline neutrophil counts between 1.3 and 1.6 across multiple samples taken when he was well, and a bone marrow examination at the time was normal. Today's routine count shows neutrophils of 1.2. He feels entirely well, has no fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers or cough, and has taken no new medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Well appearing with no pallor, oropharynx clear with no ulceration or exudate, no cervical lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation, no skin lesions or abscesses
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 1.2 x10^9/L, white cell count 3.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-175), platelets 262 x10^9/L (150-400), C reactive protein within normal limits, previous documented baseline neutrophils 1.3 to 1.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue clozapine unchanged and add lithium to raise the neutrophil count, keeping the monitoring interval as it currently stands for this patient
options.rationale: Lithium does raise the count and is sometimes used to support continued treatment, but adding it here medicates a normal constitutional value and risks masking a genuine future fall. It also brings its own toxicity and monitoring burden. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue clozapine unchanged and give granulocyte colony stimulating factor today, returning to the routine monitoring schedule once the count has responded
options.rationale: Colony stimulating factor is reserved for severe neutropenia or agranulocytosis with infection, and using it for a constitutional count exposes him to bone pain and expense for no benefit. It would also obscure the interpretation of subsequent counts. (Source: Clozapine monitoring protocols: Australian product information)
source_refs: Clozapine monitoring protocols: Australian product information

options.text: Continue clozapine under the modified thresholds of his registered protocol, increase the frequency of counts and confirm the plan with his haematologist
options.rationale: The lower thresholds of a registered benign ethnic neutropenia protocol exist precisely so that a count at his documented constitutional baseline does not end effective treatment, and this value sits at that baseline in a well man. More frequent counts with haematology oversight manage the residual uncertainty. (Source: Clozapine monitoring protocols: Australian product information)
source_refs: Clozapine monitoring protocols: Australian product information

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately and permanently, record the event as a haematological adverse reaction and start a different antipsychotic this week
options.rationale: Permanent cessation applies to genuine clozapine induced neutropenia, and applying the standard threshold to a man with a documented lower constitutional baseline removes the only drug that has controlled his illness. A recorded cessation of this type also blocks any future rechallenge. (Source: Clozapine monitoring protocols: Australian product information)
source_refs: Clozapine monitoring protocols: Australian product information

options.text: Withhold clozapine for a week while daily counts are taken, and resume it only if the neutrophil count has risen above the standard green range threshold
options.rationale: His counts have never reached the standard threshold and are not expected to, so this plan interrupts treatment indefinitely. Interruption beyond two days also mandates retitration with its own risks of hypotension and seizures. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Clozapine is the only antipsychotic with established efficacy in treatment resistant schizophrenia, and mandatory haematological monitoring exists because of the risk of agranulocytosis, which is highest in the first eighteen weeks. Standard Australian monitoring uses a traffic light system in which a neutrophil count below the red threshold requires immediate and permanent cessation with registration that prevents future rechallenge. Benign ethnic neutropenia affects a substantial proportion of people of African and Middle Eastern ancestry and reflects a constitutionally lower circulating neutrophil pool with normal marrow reserve and no increase in infection risk, most often associated with the Duffy null phenotype. Applying unmodified thresholds to these patients denies effective treatment for a laboratory finding that carries no clinical risk, so registered protocols with lower thresholds, confirmed baselines and haematology oversight allow continuation. The distinction that matters is between a count sitting at a documented stable baseline in a well patient and a genuine downward trend, which needs the standard response regardless of ancestry.
key_points: Clozapine monitoring exists because of agranulocytosis risk, greatest in the first eighteen weeks.
Standard red range results require immediate and permanent cessation.
Benign ethnic neutropenia is a constitutional low count with normal marrow reserve and no excess infection risk.
Registered protocols with lower thresholds and haematology oversight permit continuation.
A fall below a documented personal baseline still requires the standard response.
explanation.pearls: Establish and document the baseline before starting clozapine in anyone of African, Middle Eastern or West Indian ancestry, because retrospectively arguing that a low count is constitutional after a red result has already been recorded is far harder and may permanently bar the patient from the drug.

sources.label: Clozapine monitoring protocols: Australian product information
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders
